title: Effects of gold cluster intercalation in graphene: stationary waves and modified QPI features
authors: Cristina Bena, Marion Cranney, Poonam Kumari, Alberto Zobelli, Laurent Simon
abstract: Gold intercalation beneath epitaxial graphene on SiC produces a cluster phase with unusual standing waves and quasiparticle-interference (QPI) features concentrated near the graphene M points. We show that this can be explained by Au intercalation below graphene hollow sites, which induces a local scattering potential on the six surrounding carbon atoms. Within a T-matrix treatment, this ring-like scatterer produces elliptical QPI structures centered near M, in agreement with the experimental FT-STS measurements. We further show that these QPI features naturally generate the nearly stationary standing-wave patterns observed in real space. Finally, we compute the local-density-of-states contrast on and off a small cluster and show that its sign and magnitude are strongly energy dependent, consistent with the experimental observations.
summary: This paper theoretically investigates the effect of gold cluster intercalation on graphene's electronic properties by modeling the Au cluster as a local ring-shaped scatterer. Using T-matrix calculations, the authors successfully reproduce the characteristic elliptic QPI patterns observed experimentally near the M points. The findings confirm that the scattering mechanism dictates both the momentum-space signatures and the resulting energy-dependent standing wave patterns in real space.
main_problem: The study investigates the electronic consequences, specifically stationary waves and modified Quasiparticle Interference (QPI) features, resulting from gold cluster intercalation beneath epitaxial graphene.
main_result: The Au intercalation acts as a ring-like scatterer, which theoretically reproduces the observed elliptic M-centered QPI structures seen in experimental FT-STS measurements. Furthermore, these QPI features naturally generate the nearly stationary standing-wave patterns observed in real space.
method: The analysis employs the T-matrix formalism to calculate scattering amplitudes and local density of states corrections ($\deltaho$) in both momentum (QPI) and real space.
model_or_system: The system is epitaxial graphene on SiC, modified by Au clusters intercalated beneath hollow sites. The electronic structure is modeled using a $p_z$ Hamiltonian for pristine graphene, coupled to an impurity Hamiltonian describing the local scattering potential from the Au cluster.
key_observables: QPI maps (momentum space), real-space standing wave patterns ($\deltaho(\mathbf{r}, \omega)$), and energy-dependent LDOS contrast sign changes.
important_parameters: The analysis is sensitive to energy ($\omega$), particularly near the upper Van Hove Singularity (VHS) region, and depends on the geometry of the scatterer (ring/hollow site).
main_assumptions: Key approximations include using a minimal T-matrix approximation ($V_{	ext{eff}}(\omega) \simeq U\mathbb{I}_6$) because QPI features are far from Au hybridization levels. A limitation noted is that small-$q$ scattering can mask the M-point contributions in real-space calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate pristine graphene spectral functions, calculated QPI maps showing double-lobe elliptical structures near M points, and corresponding real-space standing wave patterns, alongside energy dependence of the LDOS contrast.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system (Au intercalation in graphene), develops a theoretical framework using the T-matrix formalism for scattering analysis, calculates key observables like QPI and real-space LDOS corrections, and finally compares these results against experimental FT-STS measurements to confirm the model's validity.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed quantum mechanical description of how localized impurities modify electronic band structure features (QPI/standing waves) in 2D materials, which is relevant for understanding nanoscale device physics and scattering mechanisms beyond simple continuum models.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Pristine 6NN graphene spectral function at different energies. The black dots denote the M points of the BZ.

FIG. 2. QPI patterns (first row), the corresponding double-lobe model (second row), and the resulting real-space standing waves (third row). We take U = 3eV. Compact M-centered lobes give coherent nearly stationary patterns, whereas the standing waves that correspond to extended features dephase much more rapidly in real space.

FIG. 3. Experimental QPI maps of the Au-cluster phase at two energies close to the upper VHS, ω = 0.8 eV and ω = 1 eV. The red dots denote the K points of the BZ, and the white dots denote the M points.

FIG. 4. Experimental standing-wave pattern obtained by Fourier filtering the dI/dV map measured at E = 0.8 V. The filter retains only the six elliptical Fourier-space regions cen- tered near the symmetry-equivalent M points, with their long axes approximately parallel to the M–K–Γ directions; all re- maining Fourier components are suppressed before performing the inverse Fourier transform.

FIG. 5. Top row: calculated LDOS correction for a representative three-atom cluster at selected energies (in arbitrary units), using U = 3 eV. Blue and red indicate negative and positive corrections, corresponding respectively to darker and brighter regions relative to the experimental background. Lower row: experimental plots showing the dependence of the LDOS with position at various energies. Except for E = -1.5eV, the panels describe approximatively the same spatial region on which we can identify roughly 5 clusters.
